::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

- Read a Snakemake profile and say what each line changes.
- Give rules threads, memory and time from the profile, not from the Snakefile.
- Start RegPipe on SLURM with the launcher, and recover when a run dies.
- Keep cluster details out of the repository with `REGPIPE_PROFILE` and `REGPIPE_OUTPUT_ROOT`.
- Write a profile for a cluster the lab has not used yet.

Time: 40 min
:::

## The same pipeline on a different machine

At the end of day 1 you ran RegPipe with something like:

```bash
snakemake --cores 4 --use-conda
```

On a cluster you do not want Snakemake to run `bowtie2` on the login node. You
want it to send each job to the scheduler, with the right number of CPUs, the
right memory and a time limit. None of that belongs in the rules. A rule says
*what* to run. Where and with how much is a property of the machine.

Snakemake keeps that in a **profile**: a folder with a `config.yaml` whose keys
are command-line options. `--profile profiles/longleaf` is the same as typing
every option in that file.

::: {.notes}
Ask who has submitted an sbatch job before. Most have; the point here is that
they will not write sbatch scripts for each step any more.
:::

## Two profiles, one pipeline

RegPipe ships three: `profiles/local`, `profiles/longleaf` and
`profiles/slurm-template`. Compare the first two.

::: {.panel-tabset group="site"}

### Laptop: `profiles/local`

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="profiles/local/config.yaml" lines="1-23" >}}

### SLURM: `profiles/longleaf`

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="profiles/longleaf/config.yaml" lines="1-27" >}}

### MicroCPipe on Longleaf

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="profiles/longleaf/config.yaml" lines="1-27" >}}

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The rules are the same in both runs. What changes:

- `executor: slurm` turns every job into an `sbatch` submission. Without it,
  jobs run as processes on the machine you are on.
- `cores` and `jobs` mean different things in the two places (next slide).
- `latency-wait` is 60 seconds locally and 500 on the cluster. A shared file
  system can take a while to show a file that a compute node just wrote.
  Snakemake waits this long before it decides a job failed to make its output.
- `default-resources` gives every job an account, a partition, a time limit
  (`runtime`, in minutes) and memory (`mem_mb`), unless the rule's own entry
  says otherwise.
- `set-threads` and `set-resources` are per rule. `align` gets 4 threads and
  2 GB on a laptop, 8 threads and 16 GB on Longleaf.

MicroCPipe's Longleaf profile has the same shape with bigger numbers, because
Micro-C libraries are much bigger than the course data. That is the lab
pattern: one profile per site, and the same keys in every pipeline.
:::

## Resources belong to the profile

The rule files set only `threads:`, as a default. Memory and time live in the
profile, and `set-threads` overrides the default. A dry run shows what one job
will ask for. Here is the same `align` job under each profile:

::: {.panel-tabset group="site"}

### Laptop

{{< generated name="regpipe-align-local" >}}

### SLURM

{{< generated name="regpipe-align-longleaf" >}}

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`slurm_account` and `slurm_partition` show as `<TBD>` in a dry run. The plugin
fills them in when it submits the job. The lab keeps every number out of the
rules for one reason: the same rule has to run on a laptop with 8 GB and on a
large-memory cluster node, and the person who knows the right numbers for a cluster is
the person using it. The field guide compares how the three lab pipelines do
this in [Resources only in profiles](../field-guide/conventions.qmd#resources).

Change resources by editing the profile. A `--set-resources` on the command
line does not add to the profile's block, it replaces all of it: with
`--set-resources align:runtime=1440`, every other rule loses its own memory
and time and falls back to `default-resources`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Point at `threads: 4` vs `threads: 8`. The rule file says `threads: 4`; the
local profile agrees, the Longleaf profile overrides it.
:::

## `cores` and `jobs`

| | Laptop (`profiles/local`) | SLURM (`profiles/longleaf`) |
|---|---|---|
| `cores` | `all`: the CPUs Snakemake may use at once, here | `100`: the most cores in use at once across submitted jobs, and the ceiling on any rule's `threads` |
| `jobs` | not set (an alias for `cores` locally) | `100`: the most jobs queued or running at once |
| `resources` | `mem_mb=6000`: total memory for jobs running together | not set: the scheduler handles memory |

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The trap is `cores` on the cluster. If you leave it out, Snakemake caps every
rule's `threads` at the CPUs of the job Snakemake itself is running in. The
launcher asks SLURM for one CPU (`#SBATCH -c 1`), so `align` would quietly run
with one thread instead of eight. The comment in the profile says exactly this,
and MicroCPipe's says the same.
:::

## The SLURM executor plugin

Since Snakemake 8, talking to a scheduler is a plugin. RegPipe installs it from
`config/requirements.txt`:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="config/requirements.txt" >}}

With `executor: slurm`, Snakemake writes an `sbatch` call for each job from its
resources: `runtime` becomes `-t`, `mem_mb` becomes `--mem`, `threads` becomes
`--cpus-per-task`, `slurm_partition` becomes `-p`, `slurm_account` becomes `-A`.
It then polls SLURM to see which jobs finished.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
You never write a job script per rule. If you used the old `--cluster "sbatch ..."`
option from Snakemake 7, it is gone in 8. The plugin replaces it. Its
documentation lists every resource it understands, including the GPU ones that
module 7 uses: see the
[SLURM plugin page](https://snakemake.github.io/snakemake-plugin-catalog/plugins/executor/slurm.html).
:::

## When a run dies

Cluster runs fail in ways laptop runs do not: a node goes away, a job hits its
time limit, the Snakemake process itself is killed. The launcher passes three
options to help:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--rerun-incomplete` | A job that was running when Snakemake died left a half-written output. Snakemake marks it incomplete; this option reruns it instead of stopping. |
| `--keep-going` | One sample's `call_peaks` fails; the other samples carry on. Without it, Snakemake stops starting new jobs at the first failure. |
| `latency-wait` (profile) | Wait this many seconds for an output to appear on a shared file system before calling the job a failure. |

If Snakemake was killed hard, its lock stays in `.snakemake/locks/` and the next
run refuses to start. Release it with:

```bash
bash unlock.sh
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`unlock.sh` picks the profile the same way the launcher does and runs
`snakemake --unlock`. It does not delete anything. Run it only when you are
sure no other Snakemake is running in that folder.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .exercise}

## The launcher: `RegPipe.sh`

You do not type the long `snakemake` command. The lab pipelines each have a
launcher script that works on a laptop (`bash RegPipe.sh`) and on SLURM
(`sbatch RegPipe.sh`):

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="RegPipe.sh" lines="44-83" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
In order, it:

1. picks the profile: `--profile`, then `$REGPIPE_PROFILE`, then `hpcProfile` in the config;
2. works out the output folder the same way `common.smk` does;
3. stops if the profile still has an unedited `<placeholder>`, such as `slurm_account: <account>`;
4. sources the profile's `env.sh`, which makes `python3` and `conda` available;
5. creates a venv with Snakemake in `env/` and installs `config/requirements.txt`;
6. on SLURM, puts the per-job SLURM logs in `<outputDir>/logs_slurm` and slows down submission and status checks so the scheduler is not flooded;
7. runs Snakemake with `--rerun-incomplete --keep-going -p` and anything else you passed, such as `-n`.

The `#SBATCH` lines at the top of the file are for the launcher job itself: one
CPU, 8 GB, two days. That job only runs Snakemake, which submits the real work.
:::

::: {.notes}
Step 3 is new since the first versions of these launchers. Without it, a run
with `<account>` fails much later with an sbatch error that is hard to read.
:::

## Why the launcher does not activate the venv

Look at step 5 again. The launcher calls `env/bin/python3 -m snakemake` and
never runs `source env/bin/activate`. MicroCPipe explains why:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="MicroCPipe.sh" lines="69-73" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Linux reads at most 127 characters of a script's first line, the `#!` line
that names its interpreter. When conda installs a Python tool into an
environment whose path is longer than that, it writes `#!/usr/bin/env python3`
instead of the full path. Snakemake keeps its conda environments under
`.snakemake/conda/<hash>/` inside your working folder, and on a deep scratch
path that is easily over 127 characters. Now the tool runs whichever `python3`
comes first on `PATH`. If you activated the launcher's venv, that can be the
venv's Python, which does not have the tool's packages, and the job dies with
`No module named ...`.

RegPipe follows MicroCPipe. TTpipe and ChromSimPipe still activate the venv:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="TTpipe.sh" lines="62-65" >}}

They work for the people who wrote them, on the paths they use. The field guide
lists bringing them in line with MicroCPipe as the first thing worth changing
([What is worth changing](../field-guide/conventions.qmd#ranked)). Module 6
shows the same problem from the other side: a `script:` rule without a
`conda:` env runs with the venv's Python.
:::

## Keep the repository cluster-neutral

Two environment variables let everyone in the lab use the same clone, or the
same git history, on different machines:

```bash
## in ~/.bashrc on the cluster
export REGPIPE_PROFILE=profiles/longleaf        # which profile the launcher uses
export REGPIPE_OUTPUT_ROOT=/work/users/$USER    # where a relative outputDir goes
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
With these set, `config/RegConfig.yaml` can keep `hpcProfile: 'profiles/local'`
and `outputDir: 'output'`, and nobody commits a path that only exists on one
cluster. On your laptop neither variable is set, so results go to `output/`
next to the launcher. On Longleaf the same config writes to
`/work/users/$USER/output`. Here is how `common.smk` resolves it:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" def="outdir" >}}

`REGPIPE_EMAIL` works the same way for the notification address (module 6),
and `REGPIPE_CONDA_ROOT` tells `env.sh` where your Miniforge lives if it is not
`~/miniforge3`. MicroCPipe and TTpipe use the same idea with their own prefixes
(`MICROC_PROFILE`, `TTPIPE_EMAIL`).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .exercise}

## Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="cluster"}

### Laptop

```bash
cd course-pipeline
bash RegPipe.sh -n     # dry run
bash RegPipe.sh        # profiles/local
```

### Longleaf

```bash
cd course-pipeline
## once: put your account in profiles/longleaf/config.yaml (or delete that line)
export REGPIPE_PROFILE=profiles/longleaf
bash RegPipe.sh -n     # dry run on the login node: no jobs submitted
sbatch RegPipe.sh      # the launcher becomes one SLURM job; it submits the rest
squeue -u $USER        # watch the jobs appear
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip .exercise}

Every SLURM cluster differs in the same few places. Start from the template:

```bash
cp -r profiles/slurm-template profiles/mycluster
```

The `<...>` values are the ones you have to fill in. The launcher refuses to

## Exercise 5.4: A profile for a new cluster

Write `profiles/<cluster>/` for a SLURM cluster you have an account on (or,
if you only have Longleaf, for Longleaf from the template, then compare with
`profiles/longleaf`). Work through this checklist; each item is a line in
`config.yaml` or `env.sh`.

- [ ] Scheduler: is it SLURM? (`sinfo --version`). If not, find its executor plugin first.
- [ ] CPU partition for ordinary jobs (`sinfo -s`), and its time limit.
- [ ] Account, and whether jobs need one (`sacctmgr show assoc user=$USER`).
- [ ] QOS, if the cluster asks for one on some partitions.
- [ ] GPU partition and how GPUs are requested, if you will run anything like ChromSimPipe.
- [ ] How you get conda: your own Miniforge, or a module (`module avail conda`).
- [ ] A scratch or work file system for `REGPIPE_OUTPUT_ROOT`, and its purge policy.
- [ ] A dry run with your profile, then a real run on the course data.

[Answer](../answers/05-cluster-answers.qmd#ex-5.4)
:::

## Snakemake 9

::: {.callout-note}
## What changes in Snakemake 9

The lab pins Snakemake 8.27.1 (`config/requirements.txt`). Snakemake 9.0.0
(March 2025) lists one breaking change: logging was rewritten around logger
plugins. Profiles, the SLURM plugin and the rules in this course work the same
way. Two things to check before you upgrade a lab pipeline:

- The dry-run tests in module 8 read the `Job stats` table that Snakemake
  prints. If the printed log changes, the parser in `tests/test_dryrun.py` is
  the first thing to break.
- 9.0 added `--replace-workflow-config`, which makes `--configfile` replace the
  Snakefile's `configfile:` instead of merging with it. ChromSimPipe does this
  by hand today. In 8.27.1 the two files are merged (module 6 uses that).

Upgrade on a branch, run the tests, and pin the new version.
:::

## Key points

- A profile is a folder of command-line defaults, one per site. The pipeline does not change between laptop and cluster.
- Threads, memory and time go in `set-threads`, `set-resources` and `default-resources`, never in the rules.
- On SLURM, set `cores` in the profile, or every rule gets the launcher's single CPU.
- `--rerun-incomplete` and `--keep-going` in the launcher, `latency-wait` in the profile, and `unlock.sh` after a hard crash cover most failed runs.
- The launcher runs `env/bin/python3 -m snakemake` without activating the venv, so a tool can never pick up the venv's Python.
- `REGPIPE_PROFILE` and `REGPIPE_OUTPUT_ROOT` in `~/.bashrc` keep cluster paths out of git.
